**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I sit here, staring at the blank page, the cursor blinking like a metronome counting down the seconds of my indecision. A thousand words—what a strange, arbitrary number. It feels both vast and suffocating, like standing in an empty warehouse with walls that inch closer every time I exhale.

What do you say when given permission to say anything? The mind reels. Do I unspool the thread of a half-remembered dream from last night, the one where I was running through a library where the books had no spines, only teeth? Do I confess that I still, at 32, sometimes hide in the bathroom at parties to scroll through my phone, pretending to answer an urgent message when really I’m just reading Wikipedia articles about deep-sea creatures that glow in the dark? Do I write about the way my grandmother’s hands looked when she peeled oranges, how the juice would run down her wrists and she’d laugh when I tried to lick it off like a cat?

Or maybe I should write about the weight of things. Not physical weight—the way a backpack strains your shoulders after a long hike—but the other kind. The weight of a glance held too long. The weight of a name you haven’t spoken in years, sitting like a stone in the pocket of an old coat. The weight of knowing you’ll never be as kind as you want to be, or as brave, or as interesting.

I think about the man I saw on the subway last week. He was wearing a suit that had seen better decades, the elbows patched with mismatched fabric, and he was reading a book with a broken spine. The title was in another language. He caught me looking and smiled, not the polite twitch of lips you give strangers, but something real, something that said, *I see you seeing me, and isn’t that strange and beautiful?* I wanted to ask him about the book. I wanted to ask him if he believed in fate, or if he thought we were all just colliding atoms with the audacity to call it meaning. But the train lurched, the doors hissed open, and he was gone. I still wonder what he was reading.

A thousand words. I could describe the way rain smells on hot pavement, or how my dog sighs in his sleep like he’s carrying the worries of the world. I could rant about the absurdity of adulthood—how no one tells you that the hardest part isn’t paying bills or doing taxes, but realizing that you’ll spend the rest of your life missing people who are still alive, still out there, just not *here*, not *now*. I could write a manifesto about the tyranny of to-do lists, or a love letter to the first cup of coffee in the morning, the one that tastes like salvation.

But maybe I should tell you about the time I got lost in Iceland. Not the dramatic, life-threatening kind of lost, but the quiet, disorienting kind where the road signs are in a language you don’t speak and the landscape is so vast it makes you feel like a smudge on a painting. I pulled over to ask for directions, and the woman at the gas station just laughed and said, “You’re already where you need to be.” I didn’t understand then, but I do now. Sometimes the point isn’t the destination. Sometimes the point is the way the light hits the lava fields at dusk, turning them the color of rust and old blood.

I think about the things we don’t say. The *I love you*s that get stuck in our throats like fishbones. The apologies we rehearse in the shower but never deliver. The questions we’re too afraid to ask because what if the answer breaks us? What if it doesn’t?

A thousand words. I could fill them with advice I don’t follow, or truths I’m still too cowardly to live by. I could tell you that it’s okay to be soft in a world that demands hardness, that kindness is not weakness, that you are allowed to take up space. I could remind you that the night sky is just a memory of light from stars that might already be dead, and isn’t that the most poetic thing you’ve ever heard?

But maybe, instead, I’ll just sit here a little longer. Maybe I’ll let the words come as they will, messy and unfinished, like life. Maybe I’ll admit that I don’t have any grand conclusions, no neat bow to tie around this ramble. All I have is this moment, this blinking cursor, this strange and fleeting chance to say something—anything—before the page runs out.

And so I do.
